Assistant: Of course, here is a Swiss recipe for Zopf.  Please note that this is a very specific recipe, and there are many different variations on this recipe.  I’ve tried to stick to the ones I’ve found most usefully on the internet.

Ingredients:  For the dough:

  2 1/4 pound (0.6 kg) lukewarm water (you should be able to hold it in your hands and barely feel a difference in temperature from room temperature)

  1 tablespoon active dry yeast (2 tablespoons warm water)

  1 cup (200 g) fine corn flour (we’ll use the regular sort, not the fine flour)

  1 1/4 cup (200 g) powdered sugar

  pinch of salt

  1/4 cup (60 g) unsalted butter, softened

Instructions:

   In a mixing bowl, combine the warm water and yeast. Cover with a plastic bag and let stand in a warm place for 10 minutes until foamy (or warm water with a little salt makes it easier).  Keep the yeast covered, as it will spoil.

   Add corn flour, sugar, a pinch of salt, and softened butter to the bowl and mix together with a wooden spoon or spatula.  The dough will be sticky.  If it seems too sticky, add a little warm water.  When the dough is ready, pour it into a clean, lightly floured bowl.  Cover with a clean towel and let rise in a warm place for at least one hour (up to 12).  You can see the dough rising by lifting it, and feeling the risen dough not only has more volume, but is also lighter in texture.

   At this time you can make the Streusel.

   Make the streusel by mixing together the sugar and flour.  If you have a food processor, you can use it, just be careful not to overprocess.

   Turn the dough out on a lightly floured surface and knead for a couple of minutes.  Form it into a ball and place in a plastic bag.  Allow to rise again for another hour.  Weigh the dough again, and divide it into two equal portions (three ounces each).  Shape one portion into a ball, wrap in plastic and return to the warm place where it will rise again.

   The other portion should also have risen, so make a fist with your hand and push down the other side (in our case it will be the back side).  Knead it, roll it out and repeat the process with the other portion.  If you are not very experienced, I recommend you to use the larger portion to make the loaf and the smaller portion to make the filling.

   When the dough has risen again you can work on cutting it.  Flour a clean surface and roll out each piece into a 10 inch (25 cm) round or oval shape.  You can easily make a square for the loaf and a heart for the filling.

   If you use a round shape, you can use a heart-cutting template to cut the dough into the shape of a heart.  Then you can bake the loaf in a loaf pan or a heart-shaped pan.
   
   The next step is to make the filling.  Melt the butter in a small saucepan and mix with the cornflour, sugar and salt.  Cook for a minute or two on low heat until thick.

   If the dough has risen, you can now work on cutting it and shaping it.  Cut it into the shapes requested by the recipe (heart, star, trifold, etc.).  Make the filling first, then cut out the shapes of the loaf and/or filling and spread the filling on top.
